summary:
West Pomeranian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, and no separate regional legislation on gender identity or sexual orientation is sourced for the voivodeship. Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese national, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite her identification as a woman and her warning that stopping medication would cause harm; her therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply it. Release came only after the legal-aid organisation cited Polish law, court rulings and international standards, prompting the Border Guard Commander to order her out on the basis that continued detention there posed a serious health risk. Detained foreign trans women in Poland are therefore held in male-only facilities until placement is formally challenged, and their release can depend on outside legal intervention.

Courts have proved willing to intervene on custody care. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone replacement therapy while she was imprisoned, having prescribed hormones for almost two years, and awarded EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling gives a trans visitor detained in Poland a Europe-wide human-rights remedy against denial of hormone therapy, though the remedy required litigation to enforce. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, and lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

National protection on gender-identity grounds remains weak. Poland provides no hate-crime protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; a March 2025 amendment bill that would introduce it was referred to the Constitutional Tribunal, where hearings were held in July and September 2025. A Deputy Justice Minister, Smiszek, announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024.

Legal gender recognition remains court-based and medically gatekept. Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially: in June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

The anti-LGBT municipal-resolution wave, which covered more than 80 municipalities and four voivodeship-level declarations as of March 2020, concentrated in the eastern and south-eastern parts of the country. The absence of local findings in West Pomeranian Voivodeship indicates thinner documentation rather than established safety.
tangentialFactors:
The municipal-resolution pattern is regional rather than national in distribution: the more than 80 resolutions and four voivodeship-level declarations recorded by March 2020 clustered in eastern and south-eastern Poland, a geography that does not include West Pomeranian Voivodeship. Similar local declarations elsewhere in the country signal official hostility that a visitor may encounter in other regions but is not documented here.

Both key custody findings are national, not regional. The March 2024 guarded-centre case and the July 2024 European Court of Human Rights ruling concern Polish facilities and authorities generally, so the same placement and medication risks apply wherever in Poland a trans visitor is detained.

Reform momentum is measurable but incomplete. Human Rights Watch assessed LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024, while successive hate-speech and hate-crime bills moved through the Government Legislation Centre, the Prosecutor General's office and the Constitutional Tribunal across 2024 and 2025 without a settled outcome.
localsOnly:
Polish citizens seeking legal gender recognition must proceed through the courts under a medically gated process; the sources describe no administrative or self-determination route.

Residents in same-sex couples gained a documented route to recognition of foreign marriage certificates in June 2024, when Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive of his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked it, while the absence of a domestic partnership framework remained the subject of a September 2024 European Court of Human Rights judgment calling for one.

Residents do not currently benefit from hate-crime protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; the March 2025 amendment bill introducing it sits in the Constitutional Tribunal after hearings in July and September 2025.

Local anti-LGBT resolutions affect residents in municipalities across the country, concentrated in the east and south-east, but the sources record no such resolution applying within West Pomeranian Voivodeship.

No source documents enforcement practice by the West Pomeranian Voivodeship authorities, local police, or courts on gender identity or sexual orientation grounds. Absence of local findings here reflects thinner documentation than established safety, and this record does not establish that the voivodeship is free of the national pattern.

West Pomeranian Voivodeship has no distinct sourced legislation of its own on these questions; whether any voivodeship-level declaration analogous to the eastern resolutions exists for this region is not resolved in the inventory.
